## You will need

- Our usual libraries, plus some of the map-specific ones from the pre_lab. You'll also be fetching Census data in Q3. Read the questions carefully!

## Load libraries and establish settings

**Task** Create a codeblock and load appropriate packages and settings for this lab.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(janitor)

install.packages("tidyverse")

library(tidyverse)
```

Let's explore Maryland elections, power outages and electric vehicle data and make some maps!

## Questions

**Q1.** Q1. In 2022, Maryland elected the state's first two African-American statewide office holders: Wes Moore as governor and Anthony Brown as attorney general. You want to compare the two's electoral performances. Using the `md_statewide_county.csv` file in the data folder, calculate the total number of votes for both the governor's race and the attorney general's race, then percentages for both Moore and Brown *based on the total of their respective contests*. Then calculate the difference between their percentages.

Get the geometry for Maryland's counties using tigris and, joining that dataframe to your results dataframe, make a county-level map of the differences between Moore and Brown's percentages. What is the story here, and what is the county with the most interesting results?

**A1.**

```{r}

outages <- read_csv("data/county_outages_march2023.csv")

# Examine the data
head(outages)
names(outages)
glimpse(outages)

# 2. Calculate outage rate per 10,000 customers
# NOTE: Adjust column names below if your CSV uses different names.

outage_rates <- outages %>%
  group_by(county) %>%
  summarise(
    customers_impacted = sum(customers_impacted, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_customers = sum(total_customers, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    outage_rate = (customers_impacted / total_customers) * 10000
  )

# View calculated rates
print(outage_rates)

# 3. Join outage data to Maryland county dataframe from Q1
# Replace maryland_counties with your actual Q1 dataframe name.

maryland_outages <- maryland_counties %>%
  left_join(outage_rates, by = "county")

# Check joined data
head(maryland_outages)

# 4. Create county-level map
tmap_mode("plot")

outage_map <- tm_shape(maryland_outages) +
  tm_polygons(
    col = "outage_rate",
    palette = "YlOrRd",
    style = "quantile",
    n = 5,
    title = "Customers impacted\nper 10,000",
    colorNA = "grey85",
    textNA = "No data"
  ) +
  tm_layout(
    title = "Maryland Power Outages by County",
    title.size = 1.2,
    legend.outside = TRUE,
    frame = FALSE
  )

# Display map
outage_map

# 5. Save map
tmap_save(
  outage_map,
  filename = "maryland_power_outages_march2023.png",
  width = 10,
  height = 8
)

# 6. Identify counties with highest outage rates
outage_rates %>%
  arrange(desc(outage_rate)) %>%
  print(n = Inf)

# 7. Summary statistics
outage_rates %>%
  summarise(
    average_rate = mean(outage_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    highest_rate = max(outage_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    lowest_rate = min(outage_rate, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

**Q2.** Make a county-level map to explore the number of customers impacted by power outages in Maryland from last March. Load the `county_outages_march2023.csv` file in the data folder and calculate a rate of customers with outages per 10,000 total customers for each county. Then join that dataframe to your Maryland counties dataframe you made in Q1 and create a county-level map of the results; you may need to tweak the fill scale to make the distinctions clearer. What's the potential story here? Given access to other months' outage data, what would your next steps be in reporting a story?

**A2.**

```{r}
# Load March 2023 county outage data
outages <- read_csv("data/county_outages_march2023.csv")

# Examine the dataset
head(outages)

# Check column names
names(outages)

# View dataset structure
glimpse(outages)

# Calculate outage rate for each county

outage_rates <- outages %>%
  group_by(county) %>%
  summarise(
    customers_impacted = sum(customers_impacted, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_customers = sum(total_customers, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    outage_rate = (customers_impacted / total_customers) * 10000
  )

# Display results
print(outage_rates)

# Join outage data with Maryland county boundaries

maryland_outages <- maryland_counties %>%
  left_join(outage_rates, by = "county")

# View joined dataset
head(maryland_outages)

# Check for missing outage data
sum(is.na(maryland_outages$outage_rate))

maryland_counties <- maryland_counties %>%
  rename(county = NAME)

maryland_outages <- maryland_counties %>%
  left_join(outage_rates, by = "county")

# Set map display mode
tmap_mode("plot")

# Create outage map
outage_map <- tm_shape(maryland_outages) +
  tm_polygons(
    col = "outage_rate",
    palette = "YlOrRd",
    style = "quantile",
    n = 5,
    title = "Customers impacted per 10,000",
    colorNA = "grey80"
  ) +
  tm_layout(
    title = "Maryland Power Outages - March 2023",
    legend.outside = TRUE,
    frame = FALSE
  )

# Display map
outage_map

# Save map as PNG
tmap_save(
  outage_map,
  filename = "maryland_power_outages_march2023.png",
  width = 10,
  height = 8
)

# Rank counties by outage rate
outage_rates %>%
  arrange(desc(outage_rate)) %>%
  print(n = Inf)

# Summary of outage rates
outage_rates %>%
  summarise(
    average_outage_rate = mean(outage_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    highest_outage_rate = max(outage_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    lowest_outage_rate = min(outage_rate, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

**Q3.** You've been assigned a story about the use of electric vehicles in Maryland and you want to make a map of the prevalence of electric vehicles in each county. Load the `ev_2020_2023.csv` file, which has the number of electric and hybrid vehicles per county from July 2020 and March 2023 and calculate a percentage change for each county (remember, that's `new-old/old`). Using the Maryland counties dataframe you made for Q1, make a county map showing the percentage change. What counties stand out to you? What questions do you have about the changes you're seeing?

Next, use tidycensus to retrieve county population data for Maryland from 2021 (you did this in the pre_lab) and join it to your vehicles dataframe. HINT: you may not need to join it on the county name, and you should already have the geometry!

Then, calculate a per capita rate of electric & hybrid vehicles using the March 2023 figure and the population estimate. You will need to choose the "per capita" value.

Finally, make a second county map showing the per capita rate. What counties stand out on this map? How is it different from the first one you made?

**A3.**

```{r}


# Install packages (only needed once)
install.packages("tidyverse")
install.packages("sf")
install.packages("tmap")
install.packages("viridis")
install.packages("tidycensus")
install.packages("tigris")

# Load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(viridis)
library(tidycensus)
library(tigris)

# Load EV and hybrid vehicle data
ev_data <- read_csv("data/ev_2020_2023.csv")

# Examine the dataset
head(ev_data)

# Check column names
names(ev_data)

# Examine dataset structure
glimpse(ev_data)




# Calculate percentage change in electric and hybrid vehicles

ev_change <- ev_data %>%
  mutate(
    percent_change = (
      (march_2023 - july_2020) / july_2020
    ) * 100
  )

# Display results
print(ev_change)

# Sort counties by highest percentage growth
ev_change %>%
  arrange(desc(percent_change)) %>%
  print(n = Inf)


# Check the column names in your Q1 dataframe
names(maryland_counties)

# Join EV data to Maryland county boundaries
maryland_ev <- maryland_counties %>%
  left_join(ev_change, by = "county")

# Examine the joined data
head(maryland_ev)

# Check for missing values
sum(is.na(maryland_ev$percent_change))



maryland_counties <- maryland_counties %>%
  
  rename(county = NAME)




# Set map mode
tmap_mode("plot")

# Create percentage change map
ev_change_map <- tm_shape(maryland_ev) +
  tm_polygons(
    col = "percent_change",
    palette = "YlGnBu",
    style = "quantile",
    n = 5,
    title = "EV & Hybrid Vehicle\nChange (%)",
    colorNA = "grey80"
  ) +
  tm_layout(
    title = "Percentage Change in Electric and Hybrid Vehicles\nMaryland: July 2020 - March 2023",
    legend.outside = TRUE,
    frame = FALSE
  )

# Display map
ev_change_map

tmap_save(
  
  ev_change_map,
  
  filename = "maryland_ev_percentage_change.png",
  
  width = 10,
  
  height = 8
  
)


# Retrieve 2021 population estimates for Maryland counties

maryland_population <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B01003_001",
  state = "MD",
  year = 2021,
  survey = "acs5",
  geometry = FALSE
)

# Examine population data
head(maryland_population)

# Rename population column
maryland_population <- maryland_population %>%
  select(GEOID, estimate) %>%
  rename(population = estimate)

# Display results
print(maryland_population)


# Make sure GEOID is stored as character
maryland_ev <- maryland_ev %>%
  mutate(GEOID = as.character(GEOID))

maryland_population <- maryland_population %>%
  mutate(GEOID = as.character(GEOID))

# Join population data using GEOID
maryland_ev <- maryland_ev %>%
  left_join(maryland_population, by = "GEOID")

# Examine joined dataframe
head(maryland_ev)

# Check for missing population values
sum(is.na(maryland_ev$population))


# Calculate EV and hybrid vehicles per 1,000 residents

maryland_ev <- maryland_ev %>%
  mutate(
    ev_per_capita = (march_2023 / population) * 1000
  )

# Display results
print(
  maryland_ev %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(county, march_2023, population, ev_per_capita)
)




# Set map mode
tmap_mode("plot")

# Create per capita EV map
ev_per_capita_map <- tm_shape(maryland_ev) +
  tm_polygons(
    col = "ev_per_capita",
    palette = "YlOrRd",
    style = "quantile",
    n = 5,
    title = "EVs and Hybrids\nper 1,000 Residents",
    colorNA = "grey80"
  ) +
  tm_layout(
    title = "Electric and Hybrid Vehicles per Capita\nMaryland - March 2023",
    legend.outside = TRUE,
    frame = FALSE
  )

# Display map
ev_per_capita_map

tmap_save(
  ev_per_capita_map,
  filename = "maryland_ev_per_capita.png",
  width = 10,
  height = 8
)

maryland_ev %>%
  
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  
  arrange(desc(percent_change)) %>%
  
  select(county, july_2020, march_2023, percent_change) %>%
  
  print(n = Inf)



maryland_ev %>%
  
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  
  arrange(desc(ev_per_capita)) %>%
  
  select(county, march_2023, population, ev_per_capita) %>%
  
  print(n = Inf)
```
